title: How To Live Like a Crusader Knight
author: The Western Spirit
summary: The Western Spirit distills Ramon Llull's thirteenth-century Book of the Order of Chivalry into a practical guide for modern masculine formation. The article's throughline is that medieval knighthood was never primarily about martial skill but about a man first ruling himself, overcoming pride, lust, greed, and anger before he could be trusted to wield strength on others' behalf. It draws out Llull's insistence that power exists to protect the vulnerable, that a man's character must be examined before he is given authority, and that the company he keeps will either raise or degrade him. The piece closes by connecting Llull's symbolic reading of a knight's equipment, where every weapon and piece of armor reminded him of a duty, to a call for modern men to surround themselves with physical and cultural reminders of who they are meant to be.
points: Argues the core of chivalry was self-mastery before external combat: a knight had to conquer pride, lust, greed, and anger internally before his physical strength could be trusted.
Frames strength and power as inherently obligatory rather than a personal privilege, citing Llull's principle that greater strength creates greater responsibility to protect the weak.
Highlights that knighthood required character examination before conferral, not just combat skill, because an unvirtuous man given power would 'dishonour the Order and bring ruin.'
Connects Llull's symbolic reading of a knight's sword, shield, and helmet (each representing a duty) to a modern practice of surrounding oneself with reminders of one's obligations.
quotes: The knight must therefore conquer himself first: he must overcome pride with humility, lust with chastity, greed with liberality, anger with patience, and all the vices with the opposing virtues, so that his body may serve the soul and both together may serve God and the Order of Chivalry.

It is the office of the knight to support widows, orphans and the helpless. Therefore the knight is bound by his office to protect the weak against the strong, the poor against the rich, and to be a shield between the prince and his people.

The squire must be examined as to his life, his habits, his character, and his intentions, for if a man without virtue is made a knight, he will dishonour the Order and bring ruin upon those placed under his power.

The squire who is to receive the Order of Chivalry must first confess his sins, fast, pray, and spend the night in vigil in the church, examining his conscience before God. For the making of a knight begins with the soul, not with the body.
Courage alone can never make a good knight, for a courageous fool can cause enormous damage. Therefore the knight needs wisdom.
